Waggle dance

From Wikifixture, the free test encyclopedia
This article is about honey bee communication. For the 2006 board game, see Waggle Dance (game).
Waggle dance
Performed byHoney bee workers (Apis)
PurposeSharing the direction and distance of food or nest sites
Decoded byKarl von Frisch
RecognitionNobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 1973

The waggle dance is a behavior in which a honey bee worker returning to the hive tells her nestmates where she found something valuable, such as a patch of flowers, a source of water or a possible new home.[1] The dance encodes both the direction and the distance of the target, which makes it one of the few known examples of symbolic communication in animals other than humans.[2]

The Austrian ethologist Karl von Frisch decoded the meaning of the dance in a series of experiments that began in the 1940s, and he shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen for work on animal behavior.[3]

Description[edit]

A worker performing the waggle run on a vertical comb.

A dancing bee moves in a figure-eight pattern on the vertical surface of the comb. The central part of the figure is the waggle run, during which the bee walks forward in a straight line while vigorously shaking her abdomen from side to side.[4] At the end of each run she circles back to the starting point, alternating between a turn to the left and a turn to the right, and then repeats the run.

Other workers follow the dancer closely, keeping their antennae in contact with her body. Because the inside of a hive is dark, followers are thought to read the dance through touch, vibrations of the comb and the air currents produced by the dancer's wings rather than by sight.[5]

Distance and direction[edit]

The angle of the waggle run relative to straight up on the comb matches the angle between the target and the sun as seen from the hive. A run pointing straight up means that the target lies in the direction of the sun, while a run pointing straight down means the bees should fly away from it.[6]

The duration of the waggle run encodes distance: the longer the run lasts, the farther away the target is. The exact calibration differs between colonies and subspecies, but in many studies one second of waggling corresponds to roughly one kilometer of flight.[7] For targets very close to the hive, bees perform a simpler round dance that signals that food is nearby without giving a precise direction.

Bees estimate distance with optic flow, the amount of visual motion they experience during the flight, rather than with the energy they spend. Experiments in which bees flew through narrow patterned tunnels showed that dancers overestimate the distance when the walls of the tunnel are close and richly patterned.[8]

Debate[edit]

In the 1960s the biologist Adrian Wenner argued that recruits find food mainly by smell and that the dance carries little useful information. The controversy lasted for years and led to more careful experiments.[9] Later studies using harmonic radar to track individual recruits, and robotic bees that performed artificial dances, supported von Frisch's interpretation while showing that odor also helps recruits find the exact spot.[10]

Nest-site selection[edit]

Scout bees in a swarm use the same dance to advertise potential nest cavities. A scout that has found a high-quality site dances longer and repeats more waggle runs than a scout that has found a mediocre one, so better sites attract more inspectors and eventually win the competition.[11] When enough scouts gather at one site at the same time, the swarm prepares to fly there.
